title: First after Op Sindoor: India invites Pak to SCO meeting in Delhi
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood – relations; Important international institutions, agencies and fora (SCO)
summary: India has invited Pakistan's culture minister to the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi (20–21 November), the first invite to a senior Pakistani minister since Operation Sindoor.
ideas: Bilateral freeze, multilateral engagement: no direct talks with Pakistan, but contact at the SCO, where the host must invite all members.
GS2 · India–Pakistan
India follows 'bilateral freeze, multilateral engagement' with Pakistan, inviting it to the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum (2026) even after Op Sindoor.
Civilisational diplomacy keeps people-to-people ties alive when politics is stuck.
GS2 · Soft power
Cultural forums like the SCO Civilisational Dialogue keep people-to-people channels open when political ties are frozen.
The SCO is where India raises common issues with Pakistan and Central Asia; Pakistan hosts the next summit.
GS2 · SCO / Central Asia
The SCO gives India a forum to push 'connectivity, transit and trade' that bilateral channels with Pakistan cannot.
keywords: SCO forum on culture and heritage; New Delhi, 20–21 Nov 2026
India's SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, proposed by PM Modi at Tianjin (2025), shows India shaping the grouping's agenda.
No direct talks; contact only at forums
India–Pakistan ties now follow 'bilateral freeze, multilateral engagement'.

pyqs: Directly usable: the civilisational dialogue is soft power at work, with a cultural forum inviting Pakistan even while political ties stay frozen.
India's role: using the SCO to keep dialogue open (hosting the forum, inviting Pakistan) while raising connectivity, transit and trade.
Importance for India: a platform to engage Pakistan and Central Asia that bilateral channels do not offer.
The forum showcases shared Eurasian heritage and India's outreach to SCO's Central Asian members.

practice.q: Despite frozen bilateral ties, India continues to engage Pakistan through the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). Discuss the significance of such multilateral engagement for India.
parts: Introduction: tensions with Pakistan, yet engagement through the SCO
India's engagement with Pakistan at the SCO (multi-dimensional)
Significance of multilateral engagement for India: positives (multi-dimensional)
Way forward with conclusion (10 marks, so combined)

answer.t: India–Pakistan bilateral relations have remained frozen for a decade over Pakistan's state policy of cross-border terrorism, from the Pathankot and Uri attacks (2016) to the Pahalgam attack and Operation Sindoor (2025). Yet India continues to engage Pakistan on multilateral platforms, most recently by inviting Pakistan's culture minister to the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi (20–21 November 2026).

answer.h: India's engagement with Pakistan at the SCO

pts.t: As host of an SCO event, India must invite every member state; engagement here is a matter of institutional rules, not a bilateral concession.
pts.ex: India's invitation to Pakistan's culture minister for the Civilisational Dialogue Forum, 2026.

pts.t: The SCO has kept ministerial contact alive even when bilateral visits stopped, avoiding a complete diplomatic breakdown.
pts.ex: Bilawal Bhutto attended the SCO Foreign Ministers' meeting in Goa (2023); EAM Jaishankar went to Islamabad for the SCO Heads of Government meeting (2024).

pts.t: India uses the SCO to push connectivity, which Pakistan's position between India and Central Asia makes central to any regional plan.
pts.ex: An Indian Additional Secretary flagged 'connectivity, regional connectivity, transit and trade' at the SCO national coordinators' meeting in Islamabad (2026).

pts.t: Overland transit through Pakistan is India's shortest route to Afghanistan and Central Asia; the SCO is the only forum where both sit at the same table on it.
pts.ex: Transit was among the issues India raised in Islamabad (2026).

pts.t: With bilateral trade largely suspended, the SCO keeps the idea of regional economic cooperation alive.
pts.ex: 'Trade' was part of the agenda India flagged at the SCO coordinators' meeting (2026).

pts.t: A soft, low-risk track that rests on shared heritage rather than disputed politics.
pts.ex: The Civilisational Dialogue Forum, proposed by PM Modi at the Tianjin summit (2025), on shared Eurasian heritage, art and literature.

answer.h: Significance of multilateral engagement for India

pts.k: Strategic posture: bilateral freeze, multilateral engagement
pts.t: India keeps up pressure on Pakistan over terror while avoiding the appearance of isolating itself or blocking regional cooperation.
pts.ex: Inviting Pakistan to Delhi while bilateral ties stay frozen.

pts.t: The SCO's counter-terrorism framework gives India a platform to raise cross-border terrorism before Pakistan and its partners.
pts.ex: The SCO Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) as a venue to press India's concerns.

pts.t: The SCO links India to energy-rich, landlocked Central Asian markets that matter for its trade and energy security.
pts.ex: Connectivity and transit raised alongside Central Asian members such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.

pts.t: Civilisational diplomacy projects India's cultural leadership and builds goodwill beyond governments.
pts.ex: The Civilisational Dialogue is expected to be held at one of Delhi's iconic monuments.

pts.t: Membership keeps India inside a grouping of Russia, China and Central Asia, balancing its ties with the West.
pts.ex: India's SCO coordinator described the SCO as a journey where 'Eurasian and Asian landmass member states have come together'.

pts.t: Proposing and hosting new initiatives lets India shape the grouping instead of reacting to it.
pts.ex: PM Modi's Tianjin (2025) proposal became an SCO forum hosted by India in 2026.

pts.t: Multilateral courtesy cannot substitute for an end to terror; every attack resets ties.
pts.ex: The Pahalgam attack (2025) followed years of engagement attempts.

pts.t: China's closeness to Pakistan can dilute SCO positions that India wants on terror and connectivity.
pts.ex: India's opposition to the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor, which passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.

pts.t: Decisions need every member's agreement, so outcomes are often declaratory rather than binding.
pts.ex: India declined to endorse the SCO Defence Ministers' joint statement in June 2025 because it left out the Pahalgam attack.

answer.t: India should use the SCO to keep raising terrorism through RATS, advance connectivity and culture where interests converge, and link any bilateral step to verifiable action by Pakistan against terror. Multilateral engagement thus lets India remain firm on security while staying diplomatically present in Eurasia, a pragmatic balance between principle and interest.

title: China says it is strictly abiding by pacts with India amid LAC face-offs in Arunachal
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood · GS3 › Security challenges in border areas
context: Days after the ITBP chief spoke of face-offs at several locations in Arunachal Pradesh, China said it strictly abides by agreements and conducts normal patrols. India's MEA said friction occurs when Chinese forces depart from established patrolling patterns in border pockets.
ideas: Normalisation since Galwan is real but fragile: friction on the ground keeps returning.
GS2 · India–China
Six years after Galwan, India–China normalisation remains fragile as face-offs recur along the LAC.
Dialogue at many levels (Corps Commander, diplomatic, leaders) keeps small incidents from escalating.
GS2/GS3 · Border management
Multi-level talks, from Corps Commanders to leaders, keep LAC incidents from escalating.
keywords: A persistent trust deficit outlasts every India–China border agreement.
The three stages of easing a military stand-off
Disengagement must be followed by de-escalation and de-induction for real peace on the LAC.
Steps that reduce the risk of miscalculation
Confidence-building measures reduce the risk of 'misunderstanding and miscalculation' on the LAC.
Ties must rest on the 'three mutuals': mutual respect, sensitivity and interest.
examples: Deadly clash followed by a stand-off of over four years
The 2020 Galwan clash was followed by a military stand-off of over four years.
pyqs: Recurring face-offs in Arunachal show why border infrastructure and the ITBP's role on the China border matter.
Border management needs mechanisms like Corps Commander talks to avoid 'misunderstanding and miscalculation'.
summary: Fresh face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh: China says it follows the border pacts; India says friction comes when Chinese patrols depart from agreed patterns.
evolution: Deadly Galwan clashes, followed by a military face-off that lasted over four years.
Last two years
Both sides took measures to rebuild relations.
Corps Commander talks at the Wacha-Damai border meeting point.

title: Climate justice needs quicker compensation: first Loss and Damage payout to Nepal
syllabus: GS3 › Environment; Disaster management · GS2 › International institutions; India's neighbourhood · GS4 › Ethical issues in international funding
context: The UN's Fund for Loss and Damage has allocated $21.6 million (about Rs 190 crore) to Nepal, nearly two months after devastating floods. It is the first time the Fund has earmarked a grant for a disaster-affected nation. The Indian Express argues the episode should become a case study for reforming the Fund.
ideas: Loss and damage is compensation, not charity, because it rests on responsibility for climate change.
GS3 climate · GS2 global governance
Loss and damage finance is compensation owed, not charity, because it rests on responsibility for emissions.
Speed is justice: delays raise hardship and rebuilding costs, especially for poor countries.
GS3 DM · GS4 fairness
Delayed climate compensation is justice denied: it raises hardship and rebuilding costs.
Money is short: $822 million pledged, about a third of pending claims.
GS3 · Climate finance
The Loss and Damage Fund has only $822 million pledged, about a third of pending claims.
keywords: Climate harm beyond what mitigation and adaptation can prevent
Loss and damage covers harm beyond what mitigation and adaptation can prevent.
Sharing climate burdens by responsibility and capacity
Climate justice demands that burdens be shared by responsibility and capacity.
Common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities
India's climate diplomacy rests on CBDR-RC: common but differentiated responsibilities.
Those who cause harm bear its cost
The polluter pays principle makes loss and damage a duty of high emitters.
data: Nepal emits barely 0.1% of global emissions yet suffers some of the worst climate disasters.
Pledged to the Fund, about a third of pending claims
Pledges of $822 million cover only about a third of pending loss-and-damage claims.
examples: Barely 0.1% of emissions, yet among the hardest hit
Nepal, a low emitter facing high losses, shows why climate justice is a moral question.
An ice-and-rock avalanche set off flash floods and wrecked hydropower plants
Nepal's avalanche-triggered floods show cascading Himalayan hazards that destroy infrastructure.
pyqs: Loss-and-damage finance as part of climate commitments: first grant, $822 million pledged against far larger claims.
Nepal's avalanche-triggered floods as a Himalayan climate hazard with cross-border lessons.
Nepal lost at least 10% of its hydropower facilities: infrastructure in fragile terrain.
Nepal's case shows who pays for 'development' driven by greed: low emitters, high losses.

summary: The UN Fund for Loss and Damage made its first grant, to flood-hit Nepal; the Indian Express says payouts must be faster and the Fund reformed.
